title: The Three Musketeers, Part 1
author: Alexandre Dumas
summary: Em 1625, o jovem e pobre d'Artagnan sai da Gasconha com uma espada, um cavalo velho e uma carta para o capitão dos mosqueteiros do rei, em Paris. No mesmo dia em que chega, ele marca três duelos com três mosqueteiros, Athos, Porthos e Aramis, e acaba ganhando três amigos para a vida toda. Entre lutas com os guardas do Cardeal Richelieu, um amor proibido e uma missão secreta para salvar a honra da rainha, começa uma das maiores aventuras da literatura.

chapters.title: A Young Man from Gascony
paragraphs: On the first Monday of April, 1625, a young man rode into the little town of Meung. He was eighteen years old, thin and brown, with a long face and very bright eyes. His horse was old and yellow, and it had almost no hair on its tail. When people saw the horse, they started to laugh. The young man's name was d'Artagnan, and he came from Gascony, in the south of France.

Before he left home, his father had given him three things: fifteen gold coins, the old horse, and a letter. “My son,” his father said, “the letter is for Monsieur de Tréville, the captain of the King's Musketeers. He was my neighbour when we were young. He will help you. Be brave, and never be afraid of a fight. Fight for any reason, because you are a Gascon, and Gascons are proud.”

At the inn in Meung, d'Artagnan saw a tall gentleman with dark hair and a scar on his face. The gentleman was looking out of a window at the yellow horse, and he was laughing. D'Artagnan's face went red with anger.
“Sir!” he shouted. “Why are you laughing? Tell me, and I will laugh with you!”
The gentleman looked at him coldly. “I am not speaking to you, sir.”
“But I am speaking to you!” cried d'Artagnan, and he pulled out his sword.

At that moment, the innkeeper and two of his men ran out of the inn with sticks. They hit d'Artagnan from behind, again and again, until he fell to the ground. When he woke up, his head was covered in blood. Through the window, he saw the stranger talking to a beautiful woman in a carriage. She had pale golden hair and blue eyes, and the stranger called her “Milady”.
“The Cardinal wants you to go to England at once,” the stranger told her. “Watch the Duke of Buckingham.”

Then the carriage left, and the stranger rode away in the other direction. When d'Artagnan looked in his bag, his letter for Monsieur de Tréville was gone. “That man has stolen it!” he cried. “I will find him one day, and he will pay.”

Some days later, d'Artagnan arrived in Paris. He sold his yellow horse for three coins and rented a small room under the roof of a house. Then he went straight to the house of Monsieur de Tréville. The courtyard was full of musketeers in blue coats. They were laughing, shouting, playing cards and fighting with their swords just for fun. D'Artagnan's heart was beating fast. These were the bravest soldiers in France.

Monsieur de Tréville listened to his story kindly. “I loved your father,” he said. “But I cannot make you a musketeer today. First you must serve in another regiment, or do something very brave. I will write a letter to the director of the Royal Academy. There you can learn to ride and fight like a gentleman.”
While the captain was writing, d'Artagnan looked out of the window. In the street below, he saw a tall man in a dark cloak. It was the stranger from Meung!
“Ah! This time he will not escape me!” shouted d'Artagnan, and he ran out of the room.

chapters.title: Three Duels in One Day
paragraphs: D'Artagnan ran down the stairs as fast as he could. At the bottom of the stairs, he crashed into a musketeer who was coming in. The musketeer cried out in pain, because he had a wound in his shoulder.
“Excuse me,” said d'Artagnan, “but I am in a hurry.”
The musketeer took his arm. He was a handsome man of about thirty, with a calm, noble face. “You are in a hurry, so you are rude? You are not very polite, young man.”
“I don't need you to teach me good manners!” said d'Artagnan.
“Perhaps not,” said the musketeer quietly. “My name is Athos. I will wait for you at noon, behind the convent of the Carmes-Deschaux. Don't be late.”
“I will be there at ten minutes to twelve,” said d'Artagnan, and he ran on.

At the gate, a very big musketeer was talking to a soldier. He was wearing a magnificent belt of gold across his chest, over his shoulder, and a long cloak on his back. The wind opened the cloak, and d'Artagnan ran straight into it. For a moment he was lost inside the cloak. When he came out, he saw something funny: the belt was gold only at the front. At the back it was just old leather. That was why the big man wore the cloak on such a hot day.
“Are you mad?” shouted the musketeer. “You can't run into people like that!”
“I was in a hurry,” said d'Artagnan. Then he smiled. “And now I know the secret of your belt.”
The big man's face went purple. “My name is Porthos. One o'clock, behind the Luxembourg Palace!”
“One o'clock. Very good,” answered d'Artagnan.

But the stranger had disappeared. D'Artagnan looked up and down the street, but he could not see him. He walked on slowly, thinking about his bad luck. “Two duels in one morning,” he said to himself. “And I am not even a musketeer yet!”

A little further on, he saw a group of men talking in the street. One of them was a musketeer called Aramis. He was young and elegant, with soft white hands and a gentle voice. As d'Artagnan passed, he saw that Aramis had put his foot on a small lace handkerchief. D'Artagnan wanted to be polite, so he picked it up and gave it to him.
“Here, sir. I think you have dropped your handkerchief.”

The handkerchief had a lady's name on it. Aramis's friends began to laugh and to ask questions. Aramis looked angry. “That handkerchief is not mine,” he said coldly. Later, when the two men were alone, Aramis said, “You have put a lady's honour in danger, sir. That was very stupid. I will meet you at two o'clock, at the house of Monsieur de Tréville.”
D'Artagnan walked away. “Three duels,” he thought. “If I am killed, at least I will be killed by a musketeer.”
At twelve o'clock, he arrived at the convent. Athos was already waiting. “I have asked two friends to be my seconds,” said Athos. “Ah, here they come.”
D'Artagnan turned round, and his mouth fell open. The two friends were Porthos and Aramis!
“But this is the man I am going to fight at one o'clock!” said Porthos.
“And I am going to fight him at two,” said Aramis.
Athos smiled. “Then we must be quick. We are the three musketeers, Athos, Porthos and Aramis. We are always together.”
D'Artagnan took off his hat. “Gentlemen, I am sorry, but I cannot pay all three of you, if Monsieur Athos kills me first.” Everyone laughed, and the young man pulled out his sword.

chapters.title: The Cardinal's Guards
paragraphs: The two swords had only touched twice when five men in red coats came round the corner of the convent. They were the guards of Cardinal Richelieu. The Cardinal was the most powerful man in France, more powerful even than the King, and his guards and the King's musketeers hated each other.
“Musketeers fighting duels!” said their leader, a man called Jussac. “Duels are against the law. Put away your swords and come with us.”
“There are five of you and only three of us,” said Athos quietly to his friends. “And I am wounded. We will lose, but we will not run.”

D'Artagnan made a quick decision. It was the most important decision of his life. “Gentlemen,” he said, “you are wrong. There are four of us. I don't have the uniform, but I have the heart of a musketeer.”
“You are very brave,” said Athos, and he held out his hand. “What is your name?”
“D'Artagnan.”
“Well, Athos, Porthos, Aramis and d'Artagnan, forward!” cried Athos.

The fight was terrible. D'Artagnan chose Jussac, the best swordsman of the guards. The young man fought like a tiger. He jumped and turned, attacked and moved back, a hundred times. Jussac grew tired and angry, and he made a mistake. At once d'Artagnan's sword went through his side, and Jussac fell to the ground.

Then d'Artagnan looked round. Aramis had already killed one guard. Porthos was fighting another and laughing. But Athos was very pale, and the blood from his shoulder was running down his arm. D'Artagnan ran to help him, and soon the last guard gave up. The four friends carried the wounded guards to the door of the convent and rang the bell. Then they walked through the streets, arm in arm, singing.

The Cardinal was furious, of course, and he went to complain to the King. Louis the Thirteenth was a weak man, but he loved his musketeers and he loved to win against the Cardinal. A few days later, Monsieur de Tréville brought the four young men to the palace.
“So this is the boy who wounded Jussac?” said the King, looking at d'Artagnan with a smile. “He is only a child! And how many guards were there?”
“Five, Your Majesty,” said Tréville. “And my men were only four, one of them was badly wounded, and one was this boy.”

The King laughed and clapped his hands. “Wonderful! But you must not fight duels, gentlemen. It is against the law.” Then he gave d'Artagnan forty gold coins and a place in the guards of Monsieur des Essarts. One day, if he was brave, he could become a musketeer.

With the money, d'Artagnan and his friends had a great dinner. They also found a servant for him, a young man called Planchet. Each musketeer had his own servant. Athos had Grimaud, who never spoke a word, because Athos did not like conversation. Porthos had Mousqueton, who was as proud as his master. Aramis had Bazin, who dreamed that one day his master would leave the army and become a priest.

D'Artagnan soon learned more about his new friends. Porthos loved good food, fine clothes, and talking about the great ladies who loved him. Aramis read religious books and always said that he was going to become a priest, but he also received many secret letters from a lady. And Athos was the most mysterious of the three. He was clearly a great nobleman, but he never talked about his past. He drank a lot of wine, and sometimes he sat for hours without speaking, with a deep sadness in his eyes.
“All for one, and one for all!” said d'Artagnan one evening, raising his glass.
“All for one, and one for all!” answered the three musketeers.

chapters.title: The Landlord's Wife
paragraphs: One morning, d'Artagnan's landlord came to see him. His name was Monsieur Bonacieux. He was a small, fat man of about fifty, and he looked very worried.
“Sir,” he said, “people say that you are brave, and that you are a friend of the musketeers. I need help. Somebody has kidnapped my wife!”
“Your wife?” asked d'Artagnan.

“Yes. Her name is Constance. She works at the palace. She is the Queen's dressmaker, and the Queen trusts her completely. I think they took her because of the Queen's secrets. The Queen has many enemies, you know. The Cardinal hates her.” He lowered his voice. “And there is an English lord, the Duke of Buckingham. They say that he is in love with the Queen, and that he has come to Paris secretly to see her.”
Bonacieux described the man who had taken his wife. He was tall, dark, with a scar on his face. D'Artagnan jumped up. “The man from Meung! He works for the Cardinal!”

Two days later, the Cardinal's men took Monsieur Bonacieux away too, and they put him in the Bastille, the great prison of Paris. But the same night, d'Artagnan heard a woman screaming in the room below his. He ran downstairs and found four of the Cardinal's men holding a young woman. He fought them alone, with his sword, and they ran away like rabbits.

The woman was about twenty-five, with dark hair, blue eyes and a pretty smile. “You have saved me, sir,” she said. “I am Constance Bonacieux. I escaped from the house where they kept me, but they found me again here.”
D'Artagnan looked at her, and he fell in love at once. “I will protect you, madame,” he said. “Always.”
“Then help me now,” she said. “I must go out tonight on very important business, and I need to go alone. Please don't follow me, and don't ask any questions.”

Of course, later that night, d'Artagnan followed her. He saw her in a dark street with a man in a musketeer's coat. He was mad with jealousy, and he stopped them with his sword in his hand. But the man was not a musketeer at all. He was a handsome Englishman with a proud face.
“Please, d'Artagnan!” cried Constance. “This is the Duke of Buckingham. The Cardinal's men are looking for him everywhere. If they find him, they will kill him!”
D'Artagnan put away his sword at once. “Forgive me, my lord. I will walk behind you and protect you.”

Constance took the Duke through a little door into the Louvre, the King's palace. There, in a secret room, the Queen was waiting. Anne of Austria was a beautiful woman, but she was sad and lonely. Her husband, the King, did not love her, and the Cardinal watched her every day.
“My lord,” she said, “you must not stay. If they find you here, I am lost.”
“I came only to see you, madame,” said Buckingham. “I love you. I have loved you since the first moment I saw you.”

“You must go back to England,” said the Queen. But before he left, she gave him a small wooden box. “Take this,” she said, “and remember me.” Inside the box there were twelve beautiful diamond studs on a blue ribbon. They were a present from the King to the Queen.
The Queen did not know that one of her ladies worked for the Cardinal, and that she had seen everything.

chapters.title: The Cardinal's Trap
paragraphs: In his palace, Cardinal Richelieu smiled when he heard the news. He was a thin, pale man with a small grey beard and cold, clever eyes. He called the man with the scar. His name was the Count of Rochefort, and he was the Cardinal's most loyal spy.

“Rochefort,” said the Cardinal, “the Queen has given her diamond studs to Buckingham. Now I can destroy her. Send a message to Milady in London. She must go to the next ball where the Duke will be, and she must cut two of the studs from the ribbon. Then she must bring them to me.”

A few days later, the Cardinal visited the King. “Your Majesty,” he said softly, “why don't you give a great ball at the City Hall? The people of Paris would love it. And the Queen could wear the beautiful diamond studs that you gave her. I am sure she would look wonderful in them.”

The King thought this was a good idea. He did not know about the box, but he had a feeling that the Cardinal knew something. He went to the Queen's rooms at once. “Madame,” he said, “there will be a ball at the City Hall in twelve days. I want you to wear your diamond studs.”
The Queen went white. “Of course, sire,” she said in a weak voice.
When the King had left, she fell into a chair and began to cry. “I am lost,” she said. “The studs are in London. Nobody can go to England and come back in twelve days. And who can I trust?”
Constance Bonacieux came close to her. “Your Majesty,” she said, “I know a man who can do it. He is young and brave, and he is completely loyal. He would die for me, and so he would die for you.”

That evening, Monsieur Bonacieux came home from the Bastille. He was not the same man. The Cardinal had spoken to him kindly, given him a bag of gold, and made him a spy. When Constance asked him to take a secret letter to London for the Queen, he said no. Then he ran straight to the Cardinal's palace to tell Rochefort everything.
But d'Artagnan, in the room above, had heard every word through a hole in the floor. When Bonacieux had gone, he went down to Constance.
“Madame,” he said, “I know everything. Your husband is a traitor. But I am not. Give me the letter, and I will go to London.”

Constance looked into his eyes for a long time. Then she gave him the letter and a bag of money from the Queen. “Go,” she said. “And be careful. If you come back alive, I promise that I will love you.”

D'Artagnan's heart was full of joy. He ran to Monsieur de Tréville and asked for fifteen days' leave for himself and his three friends. “I can't tell you why,” he said. “It is a secret, and it is for the Queen.”
“Then you must not travel alone,” said Tréville. “The Cardinal's men will try to stop you. Go four together. If only one of you arrives, that will be enough.”

At two o'clock in the morning, the four friends and their four servants left Paris by the road to Calais. Each man had a sword and two pistols. Only d'Artagnan knew what the letter said, and only he knew how important it was.
“All for one, and one for all,” said Athos, as they rode out of the city under the stars.

chapters.title: The Road to Calais
paragraphs: For the first hours, everything went well. The sun came up, the birds were singing, and the four friends were happy to be on an adventure. At eight o'clock they stopped at an inn in Chantilly for breakfast.
At another table there was a gentleman who was drinking alone. He was very friendly, and he asked Porthos to drink to the Cardinal's health.
“With pleasure,” said Porthos, “if you will drink to the King's health afterwards.”
“I know only one master, and that is the Cardinal!” said the stranger.

Porthos stood up and pulled out his sword. His friends could see that it was a trap, but they could not stop him. “Finish your fight and catch up with us later,” said Athos. The other three rode on, and they left Porthos fighting with the stranger in the courtyard.

Around midday, the road passed between two walls, where some men were working with shovels. As the travellers came near, the workers dropped their shovels and picked up muskets. They had been waiting for them! A bullet hit Aramis in the shoulder, and another bullet killed Mousqueton's horse. The friends rode as fast as they could and escaped. But Aramis was very pale, and in the next town he could not stay on his horse.
“Leave me here with Bazin,” he said. “I will be all right. Go! The Queen is waiting.”

Now there were only two of them. That night they arrived at Amiens. The innkeeper was very polite, too polite. In the morning, Athos went to pay the bill. A minute later, d'Artagnan heard shouting. When he looked through the door, he saw four men with guns attacking Athos. The innkeeper was shouting that Athos's money was false.
“Go, d'Artagnan!” shouted Athos, fighting with his sword in one hand and a pistol in the other. “Ride! Ride!”

D'Artagnan did not want to leave his friend. But he remembered the letter and the Queen. With Planchet behind him, he jumped on his horse and rode away. Behind him he could hear the sound of the fight, and he felt sick with sadness.
“Our friends are lost,” he said to Planchet, with tears in his eyes. “The Cardinal has been very clever.”
“They are not dead yet, sir,” said Planchet. “Monsieur Athos is the bravest man I know.”

They rode all day without stopping. When their horses fell, they bought new ones. Finally, after a long and terrible journey, they saw the grey sea and the port of Calais. But the Cardinal's men had been faster than them. The port was closed.
“Nobody can sail to England without a paper from the Cardinal,” a sailor told them. “Those are the orders.”
D'Artagnan was not ready to give up. At that moment, a gentleman and his servant arrived at the port, covered in dust. The gentleman was in a great hurry, and he went straight to the harbour master.
“That man has a paper from the Cardinal,” whispered Planchet.
D'Artagnan looked at him and smiled. “Then I must take it.”

chapters.title: The Duel at the Sea
paragraphs: D'Artagnan followed the gentleman out of the town, into a small wood near the sea. When they were alone, he stopped him.
“Sir,” he said politely, “you are going to England, I think.”
“Yes, I am. I am the Count de Wardes, and I have a paper signed by the Cardinal. What do you want?”
“I want your paper,” said d'Artagnan. “I am in a great hurry too, and I have no paper.”
The Count de Wardes laughed. “You are joking!”
“I never joke, sir,” said d'Artagnan, and he pulled out his sword.

De Wardes was a good swordsman, and he fought hard. But d'Artagnan was young and quick, and he was fighting for the Queen and for Constance. He wounded the Count three times. At the third wound, de Wardes fell to the ground. “You have killed me,” he said, and he fainted.

D'Artagnan found the paper in the Count's pocket. It said: “Let the Count de Wardes pass. Richelieu.” Meanwhile, Planchet had held de Wardes's servant by the neck until the man could not breathe. They tied him to a tree, so that he could not raise the alarm.
“The Count is not dead,” said d'Artagnan, looking at the wounded man. “I will tell someone to come and help him. I am not a murderer.”
At the port, d'Artagnan showed the paper to the harbour master. The man looked at it carefully.
“Everything is in order, Count de Wardes,” he said. “Do you know, we are looking for a young man from Gascony who left Paris four days ago? The Cardinal wants him stopped.”
“I know him well,” said d'Artagnan seriously. “He is very dangerous. If you see him, arrest him at once.” Then he walked onto a small boat with Planchet, and half an hour later they were out at sea.

D'Artagnan was so tired that he fell asleep on the deck. He was also hurt, because de Wardes's sword had cut him twice, but he did not care. The wind was strong, and the little boat flew over the grey waves. At ten o'clock the next morning, they arrived at the English coast.
“We are in England,” said d'Artagnan. “Now, to London! As fast as we can!”

He did not speak a word of English. But he wrote the name “Buckingham” on a piece of paper and showed it to people, and everybody pointed the way. By evening, he was in London, and he was knocking at the door of the Duke's palace.

The Duke was not there. He was hunting with the King of England. D'Artagnan did not want to wait. He rode out to the hunting place and found Buckingham there, on a beautiful horse. When the Duke saw d'Artagnan, he went white.
“Has something happened to the Queen?” he asked. “Is she in danger?”
“I think she is in great danger, my lord,” said d'Artagnan. “And only you can save her. Here is a letter from Her Majesty.”
Buckingham read the letter, and his face changed. “Come with me,” he said. “Quickly!”

chapters.title: Twelve Diamonds
paragraphs: Buckingham took d'Artagnan to his palace in London. They walked through many beautiful rooms until they arrived at a small, secret room. It was like a little church. On the wall there was a large painting of Anne of Austria, the Queen of France. Under the painting there was a small table with the wooden box on it.
“Here are the studs,” said Buckingham, opening the box. “I wanted to keep them all my life. But the Queen wants them back, and I will always obey her.”
He took out the blue ribbon and began to kiss the diamonds one by one. Suddenly he gave a terrible cry.
“What is the matter, my lord?” asked d'Artagnan.
“Two of the studs are gone! Somebody has cut them from the ribbon!”

Buckingham thought for a moment. Then he hit the table with his hand. “I wore them only once, at a ball a week ago. And there was a woman there, the Countess de Winter. She was very friendly to me. She came very close to me while we were dancing. It was her! That woman works for the Cardinal!”
“Then the Cardinal has the two studs,” said d'Artagnan. “He will show them to the King. The Queen is lost!”

“Not yet,” said Buckingham. “The ball is in five days. We have time.” He called his servant. “Bring my jeweller here at once! And tell the captain of the port that no ship may leave England for France. No ship, do you understand? I don't care if it causes a war.”
D'Artagnan looked at the Duke with surprise. This man was ready to start a war between two countries for the love of a woman.
The jeweller came. Buckingham showed him the studs. “Can you make two new ones exactly like these? How much time do you need?”
“Two days, my lord,” said the jeweller. “Perhaps a week, if...”
“You have two days. I will pay you three thousand pistoles for each one. And you will work here, in my palace, so that nobody knows our secret.”
The jeweller worked day and night. Two days later, he brought the two new studs. They were so perfect that even Buckingham could not see the difference.
The Duke put the twelve studs back in the box and gave it to d'Artagnan. “Here,” he said. “Tell the Queen that I have done what she asked. And now, how can I thank you?”
“You don't need to thank me, my lord,” said d'Artagnan proudly. “I am serving the Queen of France, not you. Perhaps one day we will meet as enemies, on the field of battle.”

Buckingham smiled. “You are a true Frenchman. Then go, and good luck. A ship is waiting for you. When you arrive in France, go to a small inn by the port. Say the word ‘Forward’. They will give you a fresh horse. There are four horses waiting for you on the road to Paris.”

D'Artagnan thanked him, took the box and ran to the ship. The fresh horses were ready at every inn, just as the Duke had promised. He rode day and night, and he did not stop to sleep. He arrived in Paris on the morning of the ball, dirty, tired and very happy.

chapters.title: The Ball at the City Hall
paragraphs: D'Artagnan went straight to the Louvre and gave the box to Constance. She took it with shaking hands and ran to the Queen's rooms. A few minutes later, she came back and kissed him quickly on the cheek. “The Queen is saved,” she whispered. “Come to the ball tonight. Stay near the little door behind the Queen's room.”

That evening the City Hall was full of light and music. Hundreds of candles were burning, and the great rooms were full of beautiful ladies and rich gentlemen in silk and velvet. At midnight, there were loud cries in the street: “The King! The King!”

The King arrived. He looked worried and unhappy. The Cardinal came close to him and gave him a little box. “Sire,” he said quietly, “when the Queen arrives, ask her to wear the studs, and count them. If she has only ten, ask her who has the other two. They are here, in this box.”
The King opened the box and saw two diamond studs on a piece of blue ribbon. His face went dark.
A little later, the Queen arrived. Everyone looked at her, because she looked lovely that night. And the Cardinal smiled a cold smile, because there were diamond studs on her shoulder.

The King came up to her. “Madame,” he said, “I am happy that you have listened to me. But I am afraid that two of your studs are missing. Here they are.” And he showed her the two studs from the Cardinal's box.
The Queen looked at him with surprise. “Your Majesty is giving me two more studs?” she said innocently. “Then I will have fourteen.”
The King counted the studs on her shoulder. One, two, three... there were twelve. All twelve were there! The King turned round and looked at the Cardinal. “What does this mean, Cardinal?”

The Cardinal's face was white, but he was clever and he answered quickly. “It means, sire, that I wanted to give Her Majesty these two studs as a present. But I did not dare to give them to her myself.”

“I thank you, Cardinal,” said the Queen, with a beautiful smile. “But I am sure these two studs have cost you as much as all twelve have cost the King.” The Cardinal bowed, but in his heart there was a terrible anger. Somebody had won against him, and he wanted to know who.
Nobody at the ball knew the real story, except for a few people. One of them was a young Gascon who was standing in a corner, watching everything with shining eyes.

Later, Constance came and took d'Artagnan's hand. She led him through dark corridors to a small room. A curtain hung across one wall. Suddenly, a beautiful white hand came through the curtain. D'Artagnan understood. It was the Queen's hand. He fell on his knees and kissed it. When the hand disappeared, there was a ring with a large diamond in his own hand.
Then Constance came back. “Thank you,” she said softly. “Now go home. I will send you a message soon, and then we can meet. I keep my promises.”

D'Artagnan walked home through the dark streets of Paris. He had a diamond on his finger and a promise of love in his heart. He did not know where his three friends were, or if they were still alive. He did not know that the Cardinal had become his enemy, and that a beautiful woman with golden hair would soon want him dead. Tonight, he was the happiest man in Paris.
But his adventures were only beginning.
